clips.op-0: This is Earth, seen from a million miles away.
clips.op-1: Closer. Western Europe, from a satellite.
clips.op-2: About four hundred years ago, a scientist who lived near here planted a willow tree in a pot.
clips.op-3: A grown willow can weigh more than a car. It all started as one small stem.
clips.op-4: A tree like this has thousands of leaves.
clips.op-5: Leaves are dotted with tiny openings called stomata. Air moves in and out here.
clips.op-6: Inside the leaf are cells. The green dots are chloroplasts, where the plant makes its food.
clips.op-7: And all around the leaf is air, full of gases too small to see.
clips.op-8: A tiny seed grows into a giant tree. Where does all of that wood come from?
clips.k-warmup: Every page in the Notebook Chain was written by a scientist who tested an idea. Today's page is about a willow tree. Before you read it, make a prediction. The tree slice has ten pieces. Tap Soil, Water, Air, or Sunlight to fill each piece. Then write one reason. Your prediction is saved until Part 4.
clips.k-words: These six words will help you read today's page. Tap a word sticker. I'll read it to you, and the card shows what it means. Try to tap all six.
clips.k-part1: This is the real page from 1648, written in Latin. Tap a yellow line, and I'll read it to you in plain English. Then hunt for two lines: the one where he says what he did not weigh, and the one where he says what the tree was made of.
clips.k-part2: Can air have mass? Let's test it. The ball is sitting on a kitchen scale. Press Pump to push air into the ball, and watch the number on the scale. Then decide what that tells you about the air around a leaf.
clips.k-part3: Some stores call this bag plant food. Tap the three numbers on the label to find out what they mean. Then compare the nutrients in the whole bag with the weight the willow gained.
clips.k-part4: Now run van Helmont's five years. Drag the year slider and watch both scales. He only weighed things at the start and at the end, so read those numbers carefully. Fill in the Change boxes. Then compare your tree with the evidence.
clips.k-wow: Van Helmont measured carefully, and his numbers were right. But his idea, water alone, left out something that was around the tree the whole time. Good scientists can be careful and still miss something. That's why the chain keeps going.
clips.k-assign: Now it's your turn to add a page to the chain. Answer the two Part B questions. In Part C, write what van Helmont did well and what he missed. Then use the planner to build your C-E-R.
clips.w-1: Organism. A living thing. A willow tree is an organism, and so are you.
clips.w-2: Carbon dioxide. A gas in the air. Plants pull it in through tiny holes in their leaves.
clips.w-3: Water. Plants take it in through their roots. Van Helmont gave his willow only rainwater.
clips.w-4: Leaves. The plant parts that catch sunlight and pull in air for making food.
clips.w-5: Roots. The plant parts under the ground. They pull water and nutrients out of the soil.
clips.w-6: Producer. A living thing that makes its own food. Plants are producers.
clips.l-1: I took a clay pot. I put in two hundred pounds of soil that I had dried in an oven, and I wet it with rainwater.
clips.l-2: In it I planted a willow stem that weighed five pounds.
clips.l-3: After exactly five years, the tree that grew weighed one hundred sixty-nine pounds and about three ounces.
clips.l-4: Whenever it needed water, I gave it only rainwater or distilled, very clean, water.
clips.l-5: The pot was big and set into the ground. To keep blowing dust out of the soil, I covered the top with a tin-coated iron plate full of small holes.
clips.l-6: I did not count the weight of the leaves that fell off in the four autumns.
clips.l-7: At the end, I dried the soil again. It weighed the same two hundred pounds, less about two ounces.
clips.l-8: So one hundred sixty-four pounds of wood, bark, and roots had come from water alone.
